Abstract
Determination of the electric potential of insulated conducting objects
is an important problem both theoreticaly and practicaly. For an in-
sulated conducting object in the presence of external charges or charges
distributed on the object surface, the problem of potential determination
is reformulated using a newly introduced J formalism. Using the J for-
malism, it is shown how the electric potential can be calculated exactly
for spherical objects and eciently aproximated for other object geome-
tries using geometrical properties of the insulated conducting object. This
aproach does not require calculation of the surface charge distribution
at the object surface of the calculation of the electric potential in the
surounding space. Properties and the performance of the aproach are
investigated numericaly using the Robin Hod method. Posible aplica-
tions of the aproach based on the J formalism are outlined for calculation
of capacitance of conducting objects.
1
Introduction
Electrostatics is a speci c limit of a dynamic electromagnetic situation in
which al electric charges are static and electric  elds do not vary in time.
There are numerous practicaly important phenomena and aplications
where the electric  elds are not dependent on time and the electrostatic
description is suitable. Some examples comprise high voltage insulation
[1], electric propulsion [2], design of microscale and nanoscale devices [3],
electrostatic eects in materials [4] and chemistry [5, 6], and various ap-
plications in agriculture [7] and industrial production in general [8].

Conducting objects (such as metalic electrodes) are of particular im-
portance in electrostatic systems.
When they are exposed to external
electric static  elds, the fre electric charge in conductors redistributes at
the surface of the conducting object so that its surface is equipotential,
and the resulting electric  eld in the conductor vanishes. Finding the elec-
tric charge surface density is important both theoreticaly (as an element
of understanding the electric  eld in the entire system) and practicaly
(e.g. since the electric charge surface density is proportional to the size
of the electric  eld close to the conducting body surface).
A particular clas of conducting objects are insulated conducting ob-
jects. They are not in contact with other conducting objects, and there is
no boundary condition for its surface, except the general condition that
it must be equipotential. Some examples faling in this clas objects com-
prise various oating conducting objects such as aircrafts and other aerial
devices, such as drones. Friction with the air during their motion causes
their charging, leading to a non-vanishing electric potential. Improving
the measurement of this electric potential is a mater of ongoing research
[9]. As the value of electric potential is in general not known (e.g. from
some boundary condition), it is problematic to use numerical methods
that require the de nition of boundary conditions on surfaces in the sys-
tem. A method which is very wel adapted to this kind of requirement,
used for numerical calculations in this paper, is the Robin Hod method
[10] which is described in section 2.
In this paper we develop a novel aproach towards the determination
of electric potential of insulated conducting objects.
In particular, we
show how the geometrical properties of a conducting object can be used
to determine the potential in the presence of external electric charges or
electric charges distributed on the surface of the insulated conductor. A
crucial advantage of this aproach is that it is not necesary to calculate
the electric charge distribution on the surface of the insulated conduct-
ing object or to calculate the electric potential in the space around the
conductor.
The contributions of this paper are mainly to the problem of calculat-
ing the electric potential for insulated conducting objects. Some of these
contributions are theoreticaly important, whereas others bring new prac-
tical advantages. Speci caly, the results presented in the paper comprise:
 A novel aproach to the calculation of the electric potential of insu-
lated conducting objects. This new formalism, caled the J formal-
ism, is a main theoretical contribution of the paper;
 A new derivation of some exact analytical results for a spherical
conductor obtained using the new formalism. These results present
a useful validation of the new formalism;
 An ecient and very god aproximation for the electric potential
of non-spherical insulated objects. This aproximation is the main
practical contribution of the paper, since the electric potential is
calculated directly from the geometry or from the average potential
of external point charges;
 An analysis of reasons for the eciency of the aforementioned ap-
proximation;
2


 A discusion of posible extensions of the developed formalism, such
as calculation of the electric capacity of conductors of arbitrary ge-
ometry.
The organization of the paper is the folowing. After the  rst section
which gives an introduction into the problem studied in this paper, the sec-
ond section brings a brief presentation of the Robin Hod method which
is used for numerical calculations of electric potentials and surface charge
distributions. In the third section, a novel formalism for the calculation of
the electric potential of insulated conducting objects is formulated analyt-
icaly. Using the developed formalism, in the fourth section exact analyti-
cal results for a spherical insulated conductor are presented. These results
are complemented by numerical simulations using the RH method, which
coroborate the obtained analytical results. The  fth section brings an
analysis of a number of non-spherical geometries of insulated objects and
external charge con gurations. The main practical contribution of this
paper, i.e. an ecient aproximation of the equilibrium electric potential
of the insulated conductor, is demonstrated in this section. The sixth sec-
tion contains a detailed discusion of the formalism and aproximations
presented in the preceding sections, as wel as posible new aplications
of this aproach to the ecient aproximation of the electric capacity of
objects of arbitrary geometries. The seventh section closes the paper with
a sumary and conclusions.

The Robin Hod method
One of key contributions in this paper is the demonstration that generaly
the average value of the electric potential at the surface of the insulated
conducting object produced by the external sources is a very god aprox-
imation of the equilibrium value of the electric potential. On the other
hand, the veri cation of this claim requires a numerical method capable
of treatment of conducting objects whose electric potential is not known
upfront, i.e. is not de ned by some boundary condition.
The Robin Hod method [10, 1] is a numerical method for electro-
static problems, which is especialy suitable for treating systems contain-
ing insulated conductors.
In the remainder of this section, we present
the idea behind the Robin Hod (RH) method and the role that non-
local charge transfer plays in it. In the presentation, we focus on the RH
method aplied to insulted conducting objects in vacum, although the
RH method has ben sucesfuly aplied to systems containing conduc-
tors at a  xed electric potential, dielectrics, etc. [10, 1, 12, 13].
Consider an insulated conducting object. The RH method starts with
a division of the body surface into smal surface elements (usualy tri-
angles). An initial charge distribution is chosen, in acordance with the
problem requirements (e.g. if the object is neutral, a vanishing surface
charge density may be chosen). The surface charge distribution is asumed
to be constant over each triangle. The electric potential is calculated for
each surface element. The electric potential for a triangle with a barycen-

The surface elements with the highest and lowest electric potential
values are identi ed. An amount of charge is transfered from the surface
element with the highest electric potential to the surface element with
the lowest electric potential, so that after the charge transfer the poten-
tials at these two surface elements are equal. The electric potential values
at al other surface elements are updated for contributions coming from
the change in charge at two surface elements.
The cycle of identi ca-
tion of surface elements with the minimal and maximal values of electric
potential, nonlocal charge transfer, and electric potential update is re-
peated until a prede ned precision for the condition of equipotentiality
is achieved. In the RH method, the charge of the body is explicitly con-
served which makes it especialy suitable for the treatment of insulated
conducting objects.
For conducting objects at  xed potential or homogeneous dielectrics,
precise rules of nonlocal charge transfer dier, but the main idea of the
algorithm is the same. The method is easily extended to multiple objects,
bearing in mind that the charge transfers are performed only betwen
triangles belonging to the same object. The method exhibits god con-
vergence, low computational complexity and is able to handle a very large
number of surface elements [10, 1, 12, 13].

Average electric potential of an insu-
lated conducting object in presence of charges
For insulated conducting objects of an arbitrary shape in the electric  eld
of external sources, the problem of determining their electric potential
may be conceptualy simple but practicaly demanding. As a response
to external electric  elds, the fre charges in the insulated conducting
object are redistributed on the surface of the object so that it becomes
equipotential. The  rst step is  nding this equilibrium charge distribution,
and the second step is calculating the electric potential by the integration
of contributions from al surface elements.
In this paper, we demonstrate a much simpler way of  nding the elec-
tric potential of an insulated conducting object than the one described
above. That is, this potential can be calculated exactly or very wel ap-
proximated by the average value of the electric potential of the external
sources at the surface of the insulated conducting object. From a prac-
tical point of view, this means that to  nd the wanted electric potential,

The results presented in the preceding sections show that the electric po-
tential of insulated objects can be calculated exactly or eciently aprox-
imated in the J formalism introduced in this paper. The aproximation
consists in keping only the  rst two terms in (9) and disregarding the
third, integral term. Analytical investigations of the neglected integral
term indicate that it is smal (i.e. the aproximation is god) when the
distribution of J values is close to its surface average hJi, although the
ful answer lies in the interplay of J values and charge surface density, as

As already stated, the practical advantage lies in the much simpler cal-
culation required for the aproximation of the insulated object potential.
For external charges, it is only necesary to calculate the average potential
of these charges on the surface of the object. This calculation depends
on both the object geometry and the positions of the charges. For the
case of a charged insulated object, in adition to the charge Q, it is only
necesary to know the average value hJi and the surface of the object S.
For many standard conductor geometries, these values can be calculated
(analyticaly or numericaly) and tabulated. This further simpli es and
facilitates the aplications. Concrete aplications might be expected from
the macroscale (e.g. in energy transmision or electric machinery) to the
microscale (MEMS or nanoparticles).
The limitations of the aproach can be asesed with con dence only
after the study of many insulated object geometries and charge con gura-
tions. Curently it sems that the aproximation of the potential starts to
be les precise when the external charges are close to the object and when
the object is elongated (i.e. les spherical). It is however, both surprising
and encouraging that even for very elongated objects the aproximation
works within tens of percent.
Real systems seldom contain just a single insulated conducting object.
It is therefore natural to ask if the aproach presented in this paper can be
extended to systems with multiple insulated conducting objects, objects at
 xed external potentials, or dielectrics. Here, the situation is considerably
more complicated since the charge distribution on one object is inuenced
by the very presence of other objects. The extension of this aproach wil
depend both on the deper understanding of why the aproach works for
single insulated conducting objects and on dedicated numerical analyses

Sumary and conclusions
The electric potential of an insulated conducting object in the presence
of some arbitrary  xed charge distribution is an important quantity both
theoreticaly and practicaly. For a general geometry of the insulted ob-
ject, the determination of this potential requires a numerical  nding of the
charge distribution at the surface of the object (or some other numerical
procedure of comparable complexity). In this paper, we demonstrate that
a computationaly much simpler alternative exists, and that for a range of
insulated object geometries and external charge con gurations, it gives a
very god aproximation of the electric potential value. This alternative
aproach consists in calculation of the average potential that the external
charges produce at the surface of the insulated conducting object. This
20


aproach is of purely geometrical nature and we introduce a novel for-
malism of its description based on a function J(~x) which coresponds to
an electric potential that the insulated object with a unit surface charge
distribution would produce at ~x on S.
The average electric potential of external charges on the surface of an
insulated conducting sphere is actualy equal to the electric potential of the
insulated conducting sphere in the presence of external electric charges.
This result is analyticaly proven in a novel way using a function J(~x), and
its validity is suported by numerical calculations using the Robin Hod
method. Although analytical results for the sphere have ben obtained
(or can be easily obtained) using method of images, these results have
ben obtained in a new way.
The main practical contribution of this paper lies in the aplication
of this aproach to non-spherical objects. The average value of the elec-
tric potential of external charges proves to be an excelent aproximation
of the equilibrium electric potential for various non-spherical geometries
and external charge con gurations. Although a more systematic study is
neded, the quality of the aproximation decreases as the object deviates
from the spherical shape and as external charges are placed closer to the
insulated object surface. However, even in several cases of complicated
geometries very dierent from a sphere (e.g. very elongated), the relative
potential dierence

of magnitude estimates of the electric potential of insulated conducting
objects without surface charge calculation for al practicaly important
situations. Veri cation of this posibility requires extensive future simu-
lations of various geometries and external charge con gurations.
From a formal point of view, the reason why the J formalism is so
sucesful lies in the smalnes of the third (integral) term in (9). The
histograms presented in section 5.2 provide an insight into a cancelation
mechanism making this term smal.
Inded, the distributions are cen-

contributions.
An intriguing question is how sucesfuly the aproach adopted in this
paper could be extended to problems beyond insulated conducting objects.
One promising aplication beyond insulated objects is the calculation of
electric capacities of conducting objects of arbitrary geometry.
In the
Discusion section it is shown how the electric capacity of the conducting
object can be aproximated using the average value of the J function. A
systematic investigation of this promising research avenue is left to future
work [15].
In conclusion, quantities of importance in electrostatic problems, such
as electric potential of an insulated conducting object or the electric capac-
ity of a conducting object of arbitrary geometry can be wel aproximated
without determination of the equilibrium surface charge distribution. A
geometrical quantity J(~x), interpretable as a potential that a unit charge
distribution would produce at a point ~x on the surface of the conducting
object, plays a central role in the aproach behind this aproximation.
The results presented in this paper are practicaly relevant because they
21


demonstrate an ecient aproximation scheme for some important quan-
tities in electrostatics. A theoretical contribution is in understanding why
this aproach works which opens way for posible new aplications in
electrostatics and beyond.

Abstract: Determination of the electric potential of insulated conducting objects is an important problem both theoreticaly and practicaly. For an in- sulated conducting object in the presence of external charges or charges distributed on the object surface, the problem of potential determination is reformulated using a newly introduced J formalism. Using the J for- malism, it is shown how the electric potential can be calculated exactly for spherical objects and eciently aproximated for other object geome- tries using geometrical properties of the insulated conducting object. This aproach does not require calculation of the surface charge distribution at the object surface of the calculation of the electric potential in the surounding space. Properties and the performance of the aproach are investigated numericaly using the Robin Hod method. Posible aplica- tions of the aproach based on the J formalism are outlined for calculation of capacitance of conducting objects.
